title: Own Both Sides of the Market or Someone Else Will
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0051: Email from Jag Duggal to Susan at Google (April 6, 2010)
excerptForBlog:
Hit $1B run rate last week - business is running well, could run faster. Launched new DFP product on GOOG technology stack.

On display leapfrogging Search: Big 6 agencies driving shift to allow them to add value. What prevents this from happening? Large pubs stop participating to prevent commoditization - need to find a way to stay whole. Technology adoption by agencies.

On Project Butterfly: Yahoo selling re-targeting from Search. Can we do it? Privacy issue and lots of opportunity on Remarketing using DCLK data first (e.g. Searches for flowers). No question it brings huge value but the question is privacy and timing - want to handle same way as IBA launch. Stronger proposition to pubs than Facebook Connect.

On 5 Big Bets: Yahoo is #1 - still almost double. Is Facebook the bigger threat? They have the most impressions - He who has the most impressions wins (Eric). We are not a leader in O&O inventory (except YouTube) - We don't have a set of verticals (Auto, Tech, Finance).

Platform Metrics: Pub: 50% share, Adv: 67% share. Pub side is strategic - Atlas didn't have strong Pub-side. Having both Adv and Pub side allows more seamless integration between both - zero discrepancies vs. up to 5% discrepancies.

lessonTitle: Own Both Sides of the Market or Someone Else Will
pullQuote: If you control the plumbing on both the buyer and seller side, you don't just win transactions — you define the rules of the game.
leadershipTraits: thinks in structural gaps, not just metrics
tracks competitors by product context, not just overall size
honest about where the platform is weak
moves fast but flags timing risks explicitly
situation: In April 2010, Google product executive Jag Duggal sent a short internal email reviewing the display advertising business. It covers five distinct strategic concerns in a few lines: growth trajectory, competitive threats from Yahoo and Facebook, a privacy-sensitive retargeting opportunity, and platform market share. The document is a court exhibit from the DOJ's antitrust case against Google.
insight: The sharpest line in the document is buried at the end: 'Pub side is strategic — Atlas didn't have strong Pub-side. Having both Adv and Pub side allows more seamless integration... zero discrepancies vs. up to 5% discrepancies.' Duggal isn't just praising operational tidiness. He's identifying why controlling both sides of a two-sided market is a structural advantage. A competitor with only the advertiser (Adv) side — Microsoft's Atlas — leaves a seam. Google closed that seam. That's a classic platform strategy move: reduce friction between sides of the market so deeply that neither side wants to leave. The rest of the email shows how clearly the team is mapping threats. Yahoo is described as 'almost double' on a key metric. Facebook has 'the most impressions,' and the email cites an Eric-attributed line: 'He who has the most impressions wins.' The team knows where the pressure is coming from and is naming it directly, not softening it.
application: Map your own business on two axes: which side of your market do you control well, and which side are you weak on? If a competitor can win by owning the side you don't, that's your biggest vulnerability. Prioritize closing that gap before you optimize the side you already lead.
